result: The FAS complex used for cryo-EM was pure, homogeneous, stable, enzymatically active, and structurally intact prior to grid preparation, as demonstrated by multiple biochemical and structural assays.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 provide converging evidence from size exclusion chromatography, gel electrophoresis, thermal shift assays, enzymatic activity measurements, and negative-stain EM that the FAS sample was high quality before cryo-EM grid preparation. This establishes that subsequent damage occurred during specimen preparation rather than from sample degradation.

result: Approximately 90% of FAS particles in plunge-frozen unsupported vitrified buffer suffered major structural damage, with particles lacking one-third to one-half of their density, limiting reconstruction to 9.5 Å resolution from ~8000 particles.
evaluation: Claims C17-C21 demonstrate through 2D/3D classification, reconstruction, and back-tracking analysis that the majority of FAS particles were damaged during cryo-EM grid preparation. The quantification (90% damaged) is supported by classification results shown in Figure 1, and the 9.5 Å resolution is determined by gold-standard FSC. The conclusion that damage occurred during preparation (C21) logically follows from the intact starting material.

result: Cryo-ET revealed that FAS particles adhered to both air-water interfaces (upper and lower meniscus) with asymmetric distribution, and nearly all particles in contact with the interface were damaged, flattened on one side, with the flattened regions aligned with the air-water interface plane.
evaluation: Claims C22-C30 provide direct visualization evidence from cryo-ET that particles contact and are damaged at the air-water interface. The observation of flattened particles with damage oriented toward the interface (C28-C29) strongly supports the conclusion that interface contact causes denaturation (C30). The asymmetric distribution (C25-C26) is an interesting observation, though the explanation remains speculative.

result: Subtomogram averaging and multi-reference alignment of FAS at the air-water interface showed that one side of the complex lacked density, particles attached with their long axis parallel to the interface, and vectors from particle centers to damaged regions pointed toward the air-water interface. About 86% were extensively damaged and 14% showed poor resolution, indicating most or all particles at the meniscus were damaged.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 provide quantitative orientation analysis demonstrating that the damaged side of FAS faces the air-water interface. The geometric analysis (C33, Figure 3D) is rigorous and the multi-reference alignment (C34-C35) provides statistical support for the extent of damage. The conclusion that essentially all particles at the interface are damaged (C36) is well-supported by the data.

result: Controlled air exposure experiments demonstrated that FAS is denatured at the air-water interface but remains intact when adsorbed to a solid substrate (carbon film) in liquid.
evaluation: Claims C37-C39 describe three experiments that systematically test the effect of air exposure. The observation that particles on carbon film remain intact (C38) while those at the air-water interface denature provides strong evidence that the interface itself, not simply surface adsorption, causes damage. However, the experiments are only examined by negative-stain EM, which has lower resolution than cryo-EM.

result: When FAS was prepared on hydrophilized graphene, particles strongly preferred the graphene-water interface over the air-water interface, and subtomogram averaging showed all particles were intact with no evidence of denaturation.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 demonstrate by cryo-ET and subtomogram averaging that hydrophilized graphene prevents FAS denaturation. The preference for graphene over air-water interface (C40) and the intact reconstructions (C41-C42) provide strong evidence. The resolution (17.1-24.6 Å) is lower than the single-particle results but sufficient to assess structural integrity.

result: Single-particle cryo-EM of FAS on hydrophilized graphene yielded only intact particles, achieving 4.0 Å resolution with D3 symmetry from ~28,000 particles. An unbiased comparison using 8,000 particles showed 6.4 Å resolution on graphene versus 9.5 Å in unsupported buffer, demonstrating that hydrophilized graphene works much better as a substrate.
evaluation: Claims C44-C51 provide comprehensive single-particle cryo-EM analysis showing that hydrophilized graphene preserves FAS integrity and enables high-resolution structure determination. The unbiased comparison (C49-C50) using equal particle numbers is particularly rigorous. The 4.0 Å resolution (C47) and improved particle orientation distribution (C51) demonstrate the practical advantages of the method. All claims are well-supported by the presented data.

result: Comparison to an earlier FAS cryo-EM structure (Gipson et al., 2010) showed that the 0.5 FSC resolution estimate of 7.2 Å was realistic, falling between the current 6.4 Å map on graphene and 9.5 Å map in unsupported buffer (both from ~8000 particles), with the better quality fully accounted for by more particles and D3 symmetry application.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 provide a fair comparison to prior work. The visual comparison (Figure 6—figure supplement 5) supports the assessment that the earlier map quality is intermediate. The explanation (C55) that particle number and symmetry account for the difference is reasonable, though somewhat speculative since the earlier work may have had different levels of particle damage.

result: The 4 Å resolution limit of the FAS map on graphene is likely due to inherent flexibility of the mesophilic yeast complex, as implied by comparison to a thermophilic FAS that achieved 4.7 Å from only ~4000 particles, while a less stable mycobacterial FAS required >100,000 particles for 7.5 Å resolution.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 present a reasonable hypothesis about resolution limits based on protein stability, but this remains speculative (C56 explicitly notes this). The comparisons to thermophilic (C57) and mycobacterial (C59) FAS are informative but don't definitively prove that flexibility limits the current structure. Other factors like ice thickness, particle orientation, or data collection parameters could contribute.

result: The upper and lower meniscus showed different curvatures and asymmetric protein distribution despite symmetric blotting, possibly because the lower meniscus remained in contact with air longer during blotting.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 describe an interesting observation of asymmetric particle distribution, but the explanation (C63) is explicitly speculative. The observation is supported by the data (Figure 2B), but the mechanism remains unclear. This asymmetry could have important implications for understanding specimen preparation but requires further investigation.

result: A survey of recent high-resolution cryo-EM structures prepared in unsupported vitrified buffer showed that only 5.7-19% of particles typically contribute to final maps, suggesting that up to 94% may have suffered partial denaturation at the air-water interface.
evaluation: Claims C64-C72 present an important broader implication, but the inference that low particle usage indicates air-water interface denaturation (C72) is speculative. While the FAS data support this interpretation, other factors could explain low particle yields in other studies (conformational heterogeneity, preferred orientation, ice quality, particle aggregation, etc.). The survey data (C66-C70) are accurately cited, but the causal attribution requires more evidence.

result: If hydrophilized graphene works for other proteins to prevent air-water interface denaturation, it would result in much higher particle usage, increased data collection efficiency, significantly better maps, and would be a major boost for cryo-EM.
evaluation: Claims C73-C74 present reasonable predictions about future impact, but these are explicitly speculative about generalizability to other proteins. The FAS results are promising, but whether the method works broadly remains to be demonstrated. Some proteins may not adhere well to graphene, or the background from dopant contamination may be problematic for smaller proteins.
